extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers and practitioners interested in digital rights management, cybersecurity, and corporate legal/ethical issues
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic article that summarizes the Sony BMG copy-protection/rootkit scandal (technical details, timeline, legal actions, company responses, and public reaction). It documents technical vulnerabilities, regulatory findings, and settlements arising from the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC settlement disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC settlement required Sony BMG to provide clear and prominent disclosure on the packaging of future CDs of any limits on copying or restrictions on the use of playback devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement also required reimbursement to consumers up to $150 to repair damage directly resulting from attempts to remove the software, and prohibited installing content-protection software without obtaining consumers' authorization. FTC chair criticized secret installations that create security risks as intrusive and unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer authorization before installing content-protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must obtain consumers' authorization before installing content-protection software on their systems; installation without authorization violates settlement terms and is legally problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that MediaMax could install regardless of EULA acceptance on Windows, and that the FTC prohibited installation without authorization in future. Platforms (e.g., macOS) prompting users is a relevant contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and safe uninstaller requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection software must include an effective uninstaller that fully removes the software and does not introduce further security vulnerabilities or persistent unwanted components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: XCP had no proper uninstaller; Sony's initial removal utility merely unmasked files, installed additional software that could not be removed, collected an email address, used an ActiveX control with backdoor methods, and in some cases exacerbated security problems. Uninstallers should not require risky components (e.g., unsafe ActiveX) or collect data unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on rootkit-like hiding techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial software should not employ rootkit-style hiding techniques that conceal files/processes or otherwise use methods identical to those used by malicious software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security firms (F-Secure, Symantec) and US-CERT noted that hiding techniques are the same used by malware and create security threats; such techniques lead to false positives from AV and expose users to exploitation by third-party malware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating security holes or backdoors
rubrics_metrics.description: DRM and copy-protection mechanisms must not create security holes, backdoor access, or mechanisms that can be exploited by worms, trojans, or other malicious actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russinovich and others documented that XCP created vulnerabilities exploited soon after disclosure, including worms and cheats in online games. Removal tools themselves can introduce additional vulnerabilities (e.g., ActiveX killbits were later issued).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and transparent EULA and privacy disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: End-user license agreements and privacy policies must accurately disclose installed components and any 'phone home' or data collection behavior; consumers must be informed of software included on media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russinovich noted the EULA did not mention XCP; one program phoned home even if user refused the EULA. FTC emphasized adequate disclosure so consumers can make informed purchasing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with free/open-source software licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: When incorporating free and open-source software, products must adhere to the licensing requirements (e.g., GPL/LGPL) of those components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers found apparent infringements of licenses for LAME, mpglib, FAAC, id3lib, mpg123, VLC, etc.; failure to follow license terms can lead to legal/ethical disputes and demands for remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall and consumer remedy obligations for defective or harmful products
rubrics_metrics.description: When distributed products cause harm or contain undisclosed harmful software, companies are expected to recall unsold units, offer exchanges or refunds, and provide remediation programs for affected consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sony BMG recalled unsold CDs, allowed consumers to exchange affected CDs for unprotected versions, and offered mail-in swap programs; regulators and attorneys general demanded removal from shelves and consumer notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential legal liability under spyware and deceptive trade laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributing software that surreptitiously installs or operates in a deceptive manner can trigger lawsuits and penalties under state spyware statutes and deceptive trade practices laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Texas sued under its 2005 spyware law claiming surreptitious installation; statutory penalties (e.g., civil penalties per violation) and remedies (legal fees, consumer compensation, injunctive terms) were sought and partly imposed in settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer security guidance and best practice advisories
rubrics_metrics.description: Security agencies advise consumers not to install unexpected software from media and to exercise caution when media appear to contain software components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US-CERT advised: 'Do not install software from sources that you do not expect to contain software, such as an audio CD.' Consumers should await vendor guidance or security patches and use updated AV tools to detect problematic components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public communication and remediation obligations after incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies implicated in security/privacy incidents should provide conspicuous public notices, cooperate with regulators, and take steps to alert consumers (e.g., homepage notices, advertising, online settlement information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sony BMG was ordered to place a conspicuous detailed notice on its homepage, make keyword buys to alert consumers, provide a settlement website with claim filing and lists of affected titles, and agree not to characterize settlements as court approval.
